hook.text: Every table in this course, every key, every join... none of it was obvious once.

paper.text: It all started with one paper, in nineteen seventy. So what came before it?

trees.text: In the sixties, data lived in trees. IBM's IMS, built to track parts for the Saturn Five rocket, filed each record under its parent.

walk.text: Want Ada's orders? A program starts at the top and follows pointers down.

route.text: Network databases made the tree a web, but the rule held. The program had to know the ROUTE.

broke.text: So reorganize the file... and every program that walked it breaks.

codd.text: Then, in June nineteen seventy, Ted Codd, a British-born mathematician at IBM, published an idea that sounds almost too plain.

values.text: Keep the data in tables, and link rows by value, not by pointer. Order one-oh-one is Ada's because it holds her number, one.

shuffle.text: So the database can store rows any way it likes. Shuffle them on disk, ask again... the SAME two orders.

independence.text: Codd called that data independence. A program says what it wants... not where to walk.

doubt.text: IBM wasn't sold. IMS made it a fortune, and critics doubted matching values could ever be fast.

systemr.text: So its San Jose lab built System R, to find out. It could.

sequel.text: Along the way, Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce wrote a query language that reads almost like English. They called it Sequel.

vowels.text: Trouble was, an aircraft company already owned that name. So out went the vowels... S-Q-L.

boyce.text: Boyce died in nineteen seventy-four, still in his twenties. His name lives on in Boyce-Codd normal form.

oracle.text: Here's the twist. IBM published that work, and a small California company read it closely. In seventy-nine, its Oracle was the first SQL database you could buy.

ibm.text: IBM's own arrived in eighty-one... the year Codd won the Turing Award.

berkeley-in.text: But IBM wasn't the only one reading Codd.

ingres.text: At Berkeley, Michael Stonebraker and Eugene Wong built a relational system of their own, called Ingres.

tape.text: Its code went out for the cost of a tape, and its people seeded an industry, all the way to Microsoft SQL Server.

postgres.text: In eighty-six, Stonebraker started over, on a database you could extend with your own types. He called it Postgres... as in, after Ingres.

quirk.text: One catch. It didn't speak SQL, and SQL had won.

yu.text: So in ninety-four, two grad students, Andrew Yu and Jolly Chen, gave it SQL. Hello, Postgres ninety-five.

rename.text: Volunteers kept it going, and in ninety-six renamed it. Officially, post-gres-cue-ell... but most of us just say Postgres.

tab.text: Compile it to WebAssembly, and you get PGlite, Postgres running right in your browser. It's run every query in this course.

version.text: Ask it who it is, and it tells you. Postgres eighteen point three.

upbringing.text: And it kept its upbringing. Raised in a lab and then by volunteers, not a sales team, it says no to rows that break your rules.

close.text: It's easier to design carefully on a database that takes your rules seriously... and now you know why this one does.
